The theme system is centralized in `src/theme.rs` and follows a two-stage loading process: raw YAML data is parsed into a `ThemeData` struct, then resolved into a `Theme` struct where hex strings are converted to `Color` objects for rendering.

### Theme Definition & Data Structures
*   **Color Struct**: [src/theme.rs#L160-L226](file://~/code/token-editor/src/theme.rs#L160-L226) - Defines `Color` as RGBA (u8) with hex parsing and `to_argb_u32` conversion for the renderer.
*   **Theme Struct**: [src/theme.rs#L416-L427](file://~/code/token-editor/src/theme.rs#L416-L427) - The final resolved theme containing sub-themes like `EditorTheme`, `SyntaxTheme`, `SidebarTheme`, etc.
*   **ThemeData (YAML Schema)**: [src/theme.rs#L229-L412](file://~/code/token-editor/src/theme.rs#L229-L412) - The `serde`-driven structs that match the YAML file structure.

### Theme Loading & Parsing
*   **Loading Logic**: [src/theme.rs#L80-L93](file://~/code/token-editor/src/theme.rs#L80-L93) - `load_theme` searches for user-defined themes in `~/.config/token-editor/themes/` before falling back to built-ins.
*   **YAML Parsing**: [src/theme.rs#L752-L768](file://~/code/token-editor/src/theme.rs#L752-L768) - `Theme::from_yaml` uses `serde_yaml` to parse content and then `Theme::from_data` to resolve colors.
*   **Built-in Themes**: [src/theme.rs#L15-L46](file://~/code/token-editor/src/theme.rs#L15-L46) - Themes like `dark.yaml` are embedded into the binary using `include_str!`.

### Applying Themes to Rendering
*   **Color Conversion**: Sub-themes provide `to_argb_u32()` methods or are manually converted during render loops to be used by the `Frame` buffer.
*   **Editor Rendering**: [src/view/mod.rs#L250-L300](file://~/code/token-editor/src/view/mod.rs#L250-L300) - Colors are pulled from `model.theme` (e.g., `theme.editor.background`) and passed to drawing primitives like `fill_rect_px`.
*   **Syntax Highlighting**: [src/theme.rs#L711-L750](file://~/code/token-editor/src/theme.rs#L711-L750) - `SyntaxTheme::color_for_highlight` maps Tree-sitter highlight IDs to theme colors.
*   **Drawing Primitives**: [src/view/frame.rs#L97-L263](file://~/code/token-editor/src/view/frame.rs#L97-L263) - `Frame` provides the low-level `fill_rect`, `blend_pixel`, and `draw_bordered_rect` methods that consume the theme colors.

If you’re like me, you spend hours in Visual Studio Code every day. A good theme isn’t just about aesthetics — it’s about reducing eye strain and keeping your workspace inspiring. Dark themes are my go-to, and after trying a bunch, these three are the ones I keep coming back to.

### [**Catppuccin**](https://github.com/catppuccin/vscode)

It offers multiple “flavors” (color schemes) to suit your mood, but my favorite is **Macchiato** . It has rich, warm tones and just the right amount of contrast for extended coding sessions. The pastel accents look great without being too bright, and the overall design feels modern yet calming.

Catppuccin Macchiato

What I love about Catppuccin is how customizable it is. You can tweak it to match your setup perfectly. The team behind it has done a fantastic job balancing aesthetics with usability.

### [**Minimal Kiwi**](https://github.com/pranjal-barnwal/minimal-kiwi/tree/main)

If you’re into sleek, distraction-free themes, **Minimal Kiwi** is a fantastic option. It has a minimalist design with dark backgrounds and vibrant green highlights that make your syntax pop.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

**Minimal Kiwi**

What I love most about Minimal Kiwi is how it stays out of your way. The colors are understated but functional, making it perfect for those who value simplicity over flash.

### [**One Dark Pro**](https://github.com/Binaryify/OneDark-Pro/tree/master)

**One Dark Pro** is one of the most popular VS Code themes for a reason. Inspired by the classic Atom One Dark theme, it offers great contrast, vibrant highlights, and a clean layout that works in any coding environment.

**One Dark Pro**

This was my go-to theme for years, and I still come back to it when I want something familiar and reliable. It’s polished, professional, and just works.

Section Title: 10 Popular VS Code Color Themes in 2025 > ... > How to change your color theme in VS Code?
Content:
To change your [color theme in Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/getstarted/themes) , you can open the Color Theme picker by navigating through File > Preferences > Theme > Color Theme on Windows or Code > Settings > Theme > Color Theme on macOS. Alternatively, you can use the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+K Ctrl+T on Windows or Cmd+K Cmd+T on macOS to open the theme picker directly.
Once open, you can browse through the themes using the cursor keys and select the one you prefer by pressing Enter. The changes will apply immediately to your workspace.​
Section Title: 10 Popular VS Code Color Themes in 2025 > ... > Which VS Code theme is best for eye strain?
Content:
There are many themes that implement specific colors meant to reduce eye strain, but the [High Contrast theme](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/accessibility) in Visual Studio Code is a good starting point, especially under various lighting conditions or for those with certain visual impairments.
This theme enhances visibility and reduces glare, which can help minimize eye strain during extended periods of coding​.
Section Title: 10 Popular VS Code Color Themes in 2025 > ... > Where are VS Code themes stored?
Content:
VS Code color themes are [stored within your user settings](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/getstarted/themes) . Typically, when you install a new theme, it modifies the `workbench.colorTheme` setting in your `settings.json` file located in your user profile directory. This file controls the appearance settings across your VS Code environment. You can find and modify theme settings directly in this file if you wish to make more detailed customizations​.
Section Title: 10 Popular VS Code Color Themes in 2025 > ... > Can I create my own VS Code color themes?
Content:
Yes! It’s easy to create your own custom VS Code color themes. Start by customizing your colors in your user settings, then generate a theme definition with the file in the Developer: Generate Color Theme From Current Settings command. From there, VS Code’s Yeoman [extension generator](https://code.visualstudio.com/api/get-started/your-first-extension) will help you generate the rest of the extension.
You can learn more by checking out the [Create a new Color Theme](https://code.visualstudio.com/api/extension-guides/color-theme) topic in VS Code’s Extension API section.

Section Title: Best Text Editor? Atom vs Sublime vs Visual Studio Code vs Vim
Content:
With so many programming text editors out there today, the seemingly simple task of choosing one suddenly becomes daunting and overwhelming.
While a straightforward answer to the “what is the best text editor for developers?” question doesn’t exist, in this post, I will share with you a side by side comparison between four of most popular ones out there: Atom, Sublime, Visual Studio Code, and Vim.
After reading the list of pros and cons, I hope you will have enough information to make a choice that best fits your needs.
*Disclaimer: As with any comparison, some of these views are subjective and are mostly based on my personal preferences. I’m someone who writes for the web (JS, CSS, HTML, etc.) using Sublime for Mac, so my perspective is a bit skewed towards what I’m used to. That said, I’ve tried to be as objective as possible.*

A hackable text editor for the 21st Century

Ability to add additional features to an edit is very important, and this is an area that Atom shines at. The package manager is installed by default and to make things even better, all packages are hosted on Github.
At the time of writing, they had a whopping 6,452 packages and themes available! Packages are so fundamental to Atom, that core features like Tree View and Settings View are simply pre-installed packages.

Content:
Url: https://www.sublimetext.com/
Cost: $70 license fee with free trial
Developer: Jon Skinner former Google Engineer
Platforms: OSX, Windows, Linux
Sublime was released back in 2007, so it’s had almost a decade to mature. According to Stackoverflow’s 2016 developer survey it’s the [3rd most popular Development Environment](http://stackoverflow.com/research/developer-survey-2016) .
V3 Beta is its latest version and while it’s been in beta for a long time now, don’t let that concern you. The product is actually very stable.
Section Title: Best Text Editor? Atom vs Sublime vs Visual Studio Code vs Vim > Sublime > Packages
Content:
Any Sublime user will tell you the first package they install is Sublime Package Control plugin. I think we all secretly hope that Sublime 3 will add this by default, but for now, you simply have to go to [the installation page on their website](https://packagecontrol.io/installation) and copy some incomprehensible Python and… Presto! You can now install any package easily from within Sublime.
Like Atom, Sublime has a lot of packages and themes! For me the essentials are:
[SideBarEnhancements](https://packagecontrol.io/packages/SideBarEnhancements) : without this, renaming/moving/duplicating files is not supported.
[SublimeLinter](https://packagecontrol.io/packages/SublimeLinter) : To add linters for different languages
[GitGutter](https://packagecontrol.io/packages/GitGutter) — Shows git status on the left side next to line numbers.

Content:
As mentioned before, although VSCode (like Atom) is built on Node.js, Electron, HTML, and CSS, it definitely feels fast (unlike Atom). I didn’t experience any lags when opening/changing files. Searching was also fast. I believe one of the differences between Atom and VSCode is that the UI Editor is built on Monaco (from Visual Studio Online), which might be the explanation for the performance difference. In any case, the performance is definitely on par with Sublime.

Content:

I’m still yet to take that step to fully dive in, but I think it would be a nice holiday project to configure it to meet similar standards I am used to in Sublime. After that, I think I really could stick with it for longer. The Git integration and in-editor debugger are great features that I’ve struggled with in Sublime but worked almost immediately in VSCode.

Personally, I’ve found going off the most popular plugins on http://vimawesome.com/ as a starting point.

Content:
Vim is as raw of an editor as you can get. It can be an incredibly fast, efficient development environment if you can have the patience to learn the commands. There’s a great online game http://vim-adventures.com/ which helps to teach the basic commands, like moving around files using `h` , `j` , `k` and `l` keys.

Content:
All of the above editors have their pros and cons. Personally, I’d say that in your developer’s career, you should give each one of them a shot for at least a week to see for yourself what works and what does not work for you. I hope that summarizing those four most popular text editors will make for a good starting point when considering making an editor change.

Content:
Dracula Theme is an open-source project driven by and for the community. Most apps that support the theme are contributions from our community.
As much as the team is responsible for the core theme and wants to support all available applications, we simply don't have the capacity to do it all ourselves.

Content:
1
Create a new repository based on
[this template.](https://github.com/dracula/template)
You can do it by cloning the repository or just clicking on "Use this template." 2
Build the theme using the
Color Palette below.
Edit the template info and upload the file with the theme configs to the repository. 3
Finally, [submit an issue](https://github.com/dracula/dracula-theme/issues/new)
with a link to your repository.
We will move the repo under the Dracula org and give you permissions to maintain it.

An arctic, north-bluish color palette.
A total of sixteen, carefully selected, dimmed pastel colors for a eye-comfortable, but yet colorful ambiance.
Created for **clear, uncluttered and elegant designs** following a **minimal and flat** style pattern.
For syntax highlighting it aims to ensure an **undisturbed focus on important parts of the code** , a **good readability** and a **quick visual distinction** between the different syntax elements.
Nord consists of four named color palettes providing different syntactic meanings and color effects for dark & bright ambiance designs.
[](https://www.nordtheme.com/docs/colors-and-palettes)
All colors are numbered from `nord0` to `nord15` where each palette contains a different amount of colors. The naming convention preserves the compatibility for terminal color schemes and allows an uncomplicated use as base for such.

Content:

```
#  npm
npm install --save nord

 #  yarn
yarn add nord

"editor.tokenColorCustomizations" : {

        "textMateRules" : [
        {
            "scope" : [
                "comment keyword.codetag.notation" ,
                "comment.block.documentation keyword" ,
                "comment.block.documentation storage.type.class"
            ] ,
            "settings" : {
                "foreground" : ""
            }
        } ,
        {
            "scope" : [ "comment.block.documentation entity.name.type.instance" ] ,
            "settings" : {
                "foreground" : "" ,

            }

        {
            "scope" : [
            "comment.block.documentation entity.name.type punctuation.definition.bracket"

Section Title: Contribute > Readme
Content:
Dracula Theme is an open-source project driven by and for the community. Most apps that support the theme are contributions from our community.
As much as the team is responsible for the core theme and wants to support all available applications, we simply don't have the capacity to do it all ourselves.
That's why the community is essential for this project to keep evolving. Below are some guidelines, tips, and specifications for those who want to apply the theme to any application.
Section Title: Contribute > Readme > How do I submit a new theme?
Content:
1
Create a new repository based on
[this template.](https://github.com/dracula/template)
You can do it by cloning the repository or just clicking on "Use this template." 2
Build the theme using the
Color Palette below.
Edit the template info and upload the file with the theme configs to the repository. 3
Finally, [submit an issue](https://github.com/dracula/dracula-theme/issues/new)
with a link to your repository.
We will move the repo under the Dracula org and give you permissions to maintain it.

A total of sixteen, carefully selected, dimmed pastel colors for a eye-comfortable, but yet colorful ambiance.

**Selective contrast**On a sunny summer day I love to read a book outside. Not right in the sun;
that’s too bright. I’ll hunt for a shady spot under a tree. The shaded
paper contrasts with the crisp text nicely. If you were to actually measure
the contrast between the two, you’d find it is much lower than black text
on a white background (or white on black) on your display device of choice. Black text on white from a computer display is akin to reading a book in
direct sunlight and tires the eye.Solarized reduces *brightness contrast* but, unlike many low contrast
colorschemes, retains *contrasting hues* (based on colorwheel relations)
for syntax highlighting readability. **Both sides of the force**I often switch between dark and light modes when editing text and code. Solarized retains the same selective contrast relationships and overall
feel when switching between the light and dark background modes.
Section Title: Solarized > Features
Content:
A *lot* of
thought, planning and testing has gone into making both modes feel like
part of a unified colorscheme. **16 ⁄ 5 palette modes**Solarized works as a sixteen color palette for compatibility with common
terminal based applications / emulators. In addition, it has been carefully
designed to scale down to a variety of five color palettes (four base
monotones plus one accent color) for use in design work such as web design. In every case it retains a strong personality but doesn’t overwhelm. **Precision, symmetry**The monotones have symmetric CIELAB lightness differences, so switching
from dark to light mode retains the same perceived contrast in brightness
between each value. Each mode is equally readable. The accent colors are
based off specific colorwheel relations and subsequently translated to
CIELAB to ensure perceptual uniformity in terms of lightness.

Section Title: projekt0n/github-nvim-theme > Configuration > Customize palettes and groups
Content:
Some examples of the groups that specs map would be:
 --    - syntax groups (functions, types, keywords, ...)
 --    - diagnostic groups (error, warning, info, hints)
 --    - git groups (add, removed, changed)
 --
 --  You can override these just like palettes
 local specs = {
  --  As with palettes, the values defined under `all` will be applied to every style. all = {
    syntax = {
      --  Specs allow you to define a value using either a color or template. If the string does
      --  start with `#` the string will be used as the path of the palette table. Defining just
      --  a color uses the base version of that color. keyword = ' magenta ' ,

      --  Adding either `.bright` will change the value
      conditional = ' magenta.bright ' ,
      number = ' orange ' ,
    },
    git = {
      --  A color define can also be used
      changed = ' #ffa261 ' ,
    },
  },
  github_dark = {
    syntax = {
      --  As with palettes, a specific style's value will be used over the `all`'s value. operator = ' orange ' ,
    },
  },
}

 --  Groups are the highlight group definitions. The keys of this table are the name of the highlight
 --  groups that will be overridden. The value is a table with the following keys:
 --    - fg, bg, style, sp, link,
 --
 --  Just like `spec` groups support templates. This time the template is based on a spec object.
Section Title: projekt0n/github-nvim-theme > Configuration > Customize palettes and groups
Content:
local groups = {
  --  As with specs and palettes, the values defined under `all` will be applied to every style. all = {
    --  If `link` is defined it will be applied over any other values defined
    Whitespace = { link = ' Comment ' },

    --  Specs are used for the template. Specs have their palette's as a field that can be accessed
    IncSearch = { bg = ' palette.cyan ' },
  },
  github_dark = {
    --  As with specs and palettes, a specific style's value will be used over the `all`'s value. PmenuSel = { bg = ' #73daca ' , fg = ' bg0 ' },
  },
}

 require ( ' github-theme ' ). setup ({ palettes = palettes , specs = specs , groups = groups })

 --  setup must be called before loading
 vim . cmd ( ' colorscheme github_dark ' )
```
Section Title: projekt0n/github-nvim-theme > Configuration > Customize palettes and groups
Content:
To find the list of syntax highlight groups defined for vim use the help `:help group-name` and `:help nvim-treesitter-highlights` for treesitter. If you would also like to see how Github Theme defines these highlight groups you can see [syntax.lua](https://github.com/projekt0n/github-nvim-theme/blob/main/lua/github-theme/group/syntax.lua) for vim's syntax and [treesitter.lua](https://github.com/projekt0n/github-nvim-theme/blob/main/lua/github-theme/group/modules/treesitter.lua) for treesitter. These files list out all all highlight groups and have a comment describing them. Another file to note is [editor.lua](https://github.com/projekt0n/github-nvim-theme/blob/main/lua/github-theme/group/editor.lua) which is the highlight groups responsible for how vim looks (background, cursorline, tabline, etc...).
To get more information check out Usage or the help file `:help github-nvim-theme` for more detailed information.
Section Title: projekt0n/github-nvim-theme > Configuration > Custom template values
Content:
GitHub Theme's `palettes` and `specs` can be extended with your own values. This is useful for users that want to
distinguish a spec value being used for multiple group definitions. This is best understood with an example.
`bg0` is used as the dark alternative background color. This is used in multiple areas (non-current file, status line,
normal float, etc...). If you would like to have the inactive color different then the float / statusline color you can
define your own value in the `specs` table.
```
require ( ' github-theme ' ). setup ({
  palettes = {
    --  Custom duskfox with black background
    github_dark = {
      bg1 = ' #000000 ' , --  Black background
      bg0 = ' #1d1d2b ' , --  Alt backgrounds (floats, statusline, ...)
      bg3 = ' #121820 ' , --  55% darkened from stock
      sel0 = ' #131b24 ' , --  55% darkened from stock
    },
  },
  specs = {
    all = {
      inactive = ' bg0 ' , --  Default value for other styles
    },
    github_dark_dimmed = {
      inactive = ' #090909 ' , --  Slightly lighter then black background
    },
  },
  groups = {
    all = {
      NormalNC = { fg = ' fg1 ' , bg = ' inactive ' }, --  Non-current windows
    },
  },
})
```

--  Returns a table with each colorscheme and the palette associated with it
 local palettes = require ( ' github-theme.palette ' ). load ()

 local palette = require ( ' github-theme.palette ' ). load ( ' github_dark_dimmed ' )

 print ( vim . inspect ( palette . red ))

Section Title: projekt0n/github-nvim-theme > Api > Color lib
Content:
Github Theme uses a color library internally to manipulate colors. You can use this library as well.
```
local palette = require ( ' github-theme.palette ' ). load ( ' github_dark ' )
 local Color = require ( ' github-theme.lib.color ' )

 local bg = Color . from_hex ( palette . canvas . default )
 local red = Color . from_hex ( ' #ff0000 ' )

 --  Blend the bg with red. The blend factor is from 0 to 1
 --  with 0 being full bg and 1 being full red
 local red_bg = bg : blend ( red , 0.2 )

 print ( red_bg : to_css ())
 --  ''

 --  Brighten bg by adding 10 to the value of the color as a hsv
 local alt_bg = bg : brighten ( 10 )
 print ( vim . inspect ( alt_bg : to_hsv ()))
 --  {
 --    hue = 212.30769230769,
 --    saturation = 21.311475409836,
 --    value = 33.921568627451
 --  }
```
There are a lot of useful functions to manipulate and work with colors in different color spaces.
See Usage for more information on `Color` .
